recipe.history:
The American drive-in restaurant is one of the country's most distinctive and beloved culinary institutions, a form of dining that emerged from the automobile culture of the 1920s and reached its golden age in the 1950s and 1960s. The Pig Stand in Dallas, Texas, opened in 1921, is widely credited as the first drive-in restaurant, pioneering the model of carhop service in which servers brought food directly to customers in their cars. By the 1950s, drive-ins had proliferated across the American South and West and had become the defining social space of teenage life — the backdrop for cruising culture, transistor radios, and the particular freedom of having a car. The classic drive-in burger that emerged from this culture was a study in deliberate, honest simplicity: an American cheese-melted beef patty on a toasted sesame seed bun, dressed with yellow mustard, ketchup, dill pickle slices, onion, and iceberg lettuce. Every element was chosen for shelf stability, cost efficiency, and the ability to hold in a paper wrapper for the journey from counter to car window, but the result was a flavor combination of such perfectly calibrated balance that it has never been improved upon, only complicated.

The milkshake-style special sauce on this burger references the drive-in tradition of combining ketchup and mayonnaise with sweet pickle relish — a formula that appeared in various forms at drive-ins across the country before being formalized and popularized by chains. The specific addition of a milkshake reduction to the sauce — using the vanilla shake as a sweet, creamy, dairy-rich base for the condiment — is an homage to the indivisibility of the drive-in burger and the drive-in milkshake, two things that were always ordered together and that exist in each other's flavor memory. Crinkle-cut pickles, with their greater surface area and crunch, are the correct pickle for this application because they were standard at the best independent drive-ins and because they provide more structural integrity than flat-cut slices when wrapped and carried to a car.

I grew up within driving distance of a drive-in that had been open since 1957 and had not changed its menu since approximately 1963. My parents used to take me there on summer evenings when the light was going golden and we would eat in the car with the windows down and the radio on. The speakers were still mounted on poles and you still had to wind your window back up to clip the speaker to it, and the carhops were teenagers who didn't entirely understand the historical gravity of what they were perpetuating. The burgers were wrapped in waxed paper and the shakes came in heavy paper cups with the name of the drive-in printed in a font that hadn't been updated since the Eisenhower administration. They were the best burgers I have ever eaten in a car, and I have been trying to replicate them ever since.

The drive-in burger tradition was built on well-done patties — the smash burger and griddle culture of those institutions prioritized speed and food safety in an era before temperature probes and food safety science had fully developed. But this recipe honors the spirit of the drive-in while correcting its one systematic shortcoming. A medium-rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, with its proper pink center and self-basting rendered fat, elevates everything the drive-in burger was trying to be. The American cheese melts more beautifully over a medium-rare patty because there is still steam and moisture rising from the interior; the special sauce mingles with the beef juices rather than pooling on a dry surface. The nostalgia is preserved. The result is better than memory.
ingredients: 1 large egg plus 1 for egg wash
2 scoops (about 1 cup) good-quality vanilla ice cream
1/2 cup mayonnaise, homemade or best quality
For the homemade mayonnaise (if making from scratch):
4 slices American cheese (the real diner-style, individually wrapped)
1/2 white onion, very thinly sliced into rings
instructions: 1. Make the crinkle-cut pickles (at least 2 hours ahead, ideally overnight): Using a crinkle cutter or waffle blade on a mandoline, slice Kirby cucumbers into 1/4-inch coins. Combine vinegar, water, sugar, salt, dill seed, mustard seed, celery seed, and garlic in a saucepan; bring to a boil, stirring to dissolve. Pack cucumber slices into a clean jar with fresh dill. Pour hot brine over cucumbers; cool to room temperature, then refrigerate. Use after at least 2 hours.

2. Make the sesame buns: Bloom yeast in warm milk with sugar for 5 minutes. Combine flour and salt in a stand mixer. Add yeast mixture, softened butter, and egg; mix with dough hook 8–10 minutes until smooth. Cover; rise 1–1.5 hours until doubled.

3. Divide into 6 equal balls; shape into tight rounds. Place on parchment-lined baking sheet; proof 45 minutes. Brush with egg wash; scatter sesame seeds. Bake at 375°F for 15–17 minutes until golden. Cool.
4. Make the homemade mayonnaise: Whisk egg yolks and Dijon together. Stream in oil very slowly, whisking constantly, until thick and emulsified. Whisk in vinegar, lemon juice, and salt.

5. Make the milkshake special sauce: Blend milk and vanilla ice cream in a blender until smooth — this is your milkshake base. Measure 3 tbsp of this milkshake and combine in a bowl with mayonnaise, ketchup, relish, yellow mustard, vinegar, garlic powder, onion powder, and salt. Whisk until smooth. Refrigerate.
6. Form the patties: Season ground chuck with salt, pepper, and onion powder. Divide into 4 equal portions (about 8 oz each). Shape into 4.5-inch patties with a center dimple. Refrigerate 20 minutes.
7. Heat a cast-iron skillet or griddle over high heat. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Cook patties undisturbed 3–4 minutes until a deep brown crust forms.

8. Flip each patty; immediately lay one slice of American cheese over each. Cook 2–3 more minutes. Target internal temperature 130–135°F for medium rare. Remove, tent loosely with foil, rest 3 minutes. The American cheese will melt into a perfect shiny blanket.
9. Toast sesame buns cut-side down in butter over medium heat until golden, about 90 seconds.

10. Assemble in the classic drive-in tradition: Spread milkshake special sauce generously on both cut sides of the bun. Add iceberg lettuce shreds to the bottom bun. Place tomato slices; season with salt. Place the American cheese-melted patty. Add crinkle-cut pickles. Add white onion rings. Optionally add a squirt of yellow mustard or ketchup. Crown with the top bun.
11. Wrap loosely in waxed paper for 60 seconds if you want the full drive-in experience — the gentle steam softens the bun slightly and melds the flavors. Unwrap and serve.
12. Serve with remaining vanilla milkshake and extra special sauce on the side.
